intro: Only 1 in 10 AI users report major benefits, another wave of high-profile AI products has hit the graveyard, and Pennsylvania is stepping in with new disclosure rules — it's a day that underscores how the industry is still searching for what actually works and who gets to set the guardrails. But it's not all skepticism: Block's eerily human voice model and a new crop of AI agents living in your text messages show the technology keeps pushing into surprising new territory. Plus, the BBC found a delightfully low-tech way to prove its nature footage is real — just leave the imperfections in.

stories.title: Van Jones discusses bridging political divides at Charter Workplace Summit; new AI Pulse research finds only 1 in 10 AI users see major benefits
stories.summary: Van Jones spoke at the Charter Workplace Summit 2026 about how fragmented media feeds drive workplace political division. Separately, Charter's AI Pulse research found only about 1 in 10 AI users say the technology significantly improves both their work and lives, with agency over AI integration being the strongest predictor of benefit. Additional findings include a gender gap in AI-exposed job growth, a 91% spike in AI safety job openings, and NYC's $10 million AI job training center.
stories.opinion: The AI Pulse finding that personal agency over AI adoption matters more than the tool itself is a useful counterpoint to top-down rollout strategies.

stories.title: TechCrunch catalogs the AI graveyard: notable failures from Character.ai to Sora
stories.summary: TechCrunch published a running list of notable AI failures including Relay (workflow automation, shut down August 2026), Character.ai (bankruptcy after five years), OpenAI's failed ChatGPT super-app redesign and shuttered ChatGPT Atlas browser, Sora's March 2026 shutdown due to costs, and Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI improvements that led to a $250 million settlement over iPhone 16 marketing claims.
stories.opinion: A sobering catalog that underscores how even well-funded AI bets fail when they lack clear product-market fit or sustainable unit economics.

stories.title: Blue Planet III keeps imperfect footage to prove it's real in the age of AI
stories.summary: BBC's Blue Planet III is deliberately keeping imperfect shots — plankton in the water, boats in frame, suboptimal conditions — that would have been cut in previous series. Executive Producer Elizabeth White says this proves the footage is authentic, since AI content tends to look overly polished. The series showcases real animal behaviors including dolphins using sea sponges as tools and inter-species fish communication.
stories.opinion: A striking admission that authenticity now requires visible imperfection — the 'uncanny valley' problem inverted.

stories.title: Block's Dessa voice model sounds eerily human, trained entirely on speech
stories.summary: Block released Dessa, a full-duplex speech-to-speech voice model trained entirely on human speech that produces natural laughs, pauses, and emotional expressions. It can run locally on consumer hardware like a MacBook M4 Max. Block is seeking safety researchers to test it before public release and sees potential applications in powering business and consumer voice experiences at lower cost.
stories.opinion: Running a convincingly human voice model locally on consumer hardware is a meaningful threshold — it democratizes the capability while making safety review harder to enforce. Where coverage differs: The Verge reports Dessa was compared against OpenAI's GPT-Live-1 with Block claiming it sounds more natural but demos showing occasional awkwardness; TechCrunch emphasizes the eerily human quality without noting awkwardness

stories.title: Pennsylvania signs law requiring disclosure labels on AI-generated ads
stories.summary: Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, requiring AI-generated advertisements to carry disclosure labels across all formats including images, video, audio, and text. Labels must match the ad's format. The law applies regardless of where an ad was created if it runs in Pennsylvania. Notable loopholes include subjective definitions of 'significantly modified,' carve-outs for parody and satire, and a narrow trigger limited to content creating 'false consumer perception' about products or services.
stories.opinion: A meaningful first step, but the loopholes — especially the subjective 'significantly modified' threshold — may limit enforcement and invite creative compliance workarounds.

stories.title: AI agents that live in your text messages are a growing product category
stories.summary: TechCrunch profiles AI agents that operate through SMS, iMessage, and RCS rather than dedicated apps. Notable examples include Ask Proxy ($1/day, proactively anticipates needs), Caddy (turns scattered phone info into tasks via iMessage/RCS), and Comma (manages tasks across Signal, Telegram, and WeChat). Instinct is the highest-profile player at a $10 billion valuation after raising $1 billion. The shared premise: text an agent like a friend instead of downloading another app.
stories.opinion: The messaging-native approach cleverly sidesteps app fatigue, but the category's long-term viability depends on whether these agents can maintain utility as phone OS-level AI assistants improve.

tweet_headlines.author: Sumanth_077
tweet_headlines.headline: Google open-sourced __Harness²__, a framework that recursively improves agent scaffolding at both the task and cross-task level — no model retraining required.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Google open-sourced Harness²!

Harness² is a framework for recursively improving the harness around an agent while keeping the underlying model weights fixed.

The interesting part is that it does this at two different levels.

For the current task, Harness² uses a Propose → Probe → Compose loop. It proposes changes to the harness, runs those variants on the same task, compares how the executions behave, and then composes a better harness from that evidence.

That is the task-level recursion.

But the process does not reset after every task.

Harness² also keeps the harnesses it adopted and the lessons supported by execution evidence, then uses those to guide how future harnesses should be improved on new tasks.

That is the harnessing-level recursion.

So one loop improves the harness for the task in front of the agent.

The second loop improves how the system learns to build better harnesses over time.

The editable harness itself can include the system prompt, guardrails, memory, tool guidance, subagents, skills, scripts, and plugins.

You can also run the recursion in two ways:

Parallel recursion explores more candidate harnesses.

Sequential recursion carries the refined harness and accumulated evidence through multiple Propose → Probe → Compose steps.

Google reports that even a single Harness² step improved GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash across JobBench, LAB, and WorkBuddy-Bench, with larger task-level recursion budgets bringing further gains.

That is what makes Harness² more interesting than just another agent framework.

It is treating the harness itself as something that can be iteratively improved from execution evidence, both within a task and across tasks.

100% open source.

I’ve shared the GitHub repo in the comments!

tweet_headlines.author: courtlinholt
tweet_headlines.headline: Most corporate AI upskilling is just __Duolingo streaks in disguise__, and spacing research (Cepeda et al., 2008) points to a better approach: longer gaps for longer retention horizons.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Your AI upskilling program is probably a Duolingo streak.

Completion badges. Seven-day challenges. A dashboard proudly reporting that most staff are "trained."

Gencay's (LearnAIWithMe) newest notebook collects the language-acquisition research, and it points away from streaks. What works is hours of input you can understand, plus well-spaced review.

The spacing evidence is the strongest part. Cepeda et al. (2008, Psychological Science) found that the best gap between study sessions depends on how long you need to retain the material: longer horizon, longer gaps. Krashen's "comprehensible input" idea is also in the notebook. It's influential but still debated among second-language researchers, so use it as a heuristic, not a law.

If you're an engineer, learn a new framework the way polyglots learn a language. Read real codebases slightly above your level. Re-implement from memory a week later, then a month later.

If you own AI enablement, build literacy around spacing, not sprints. Replace the one-day workshop with short sessions on real internal workflows, revisited at one week, one month and three months. Then measure who is actually shipping with AI at day 90, not who attended. If day-90 usage looks like day-one usage, the program trained attendance.

Notebook: notebooklm. google. com/notebook/c5b816da-9b53-4bdb-a68c-320cd07fe968

tweet_headlines.author: cherry_mx_reds
tweet_headlines.headline: Anthropic now advises companies to __remove unnecessary subagents__, with one customer seeing ~2x faster execution from a single skilled agent over complex multi-agent systems.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Anthropic is now recommending that companies REMOVE unnecessary subagents from their AI systems.

This is a pretty significant shift in agent architecture, with their team finding that a single agent equipped with skills can frequently outperform complex multi-agent systems, and one customer seeing roughly 2x faster execution.

The emerging rules of thumb:

→ Skills: Teach the agent HOW to do something, including procedures, expertise, and instructions.

→ Tools / MCP: Give the agent the ability to DO things through APIs, actions, and live data.

→ Subagents: Use for parallel work, isolated context, or tasks a single agent struggles with.

The interesting part is progressive disclosure. Instead of spawning specialized agents or stuffing everything into a giant prompt, one agent discovers and loads skills and tools as needed.

Their advice is to fold existing subagents into the main loop, turn their instructions into skills, expose their actions as tools, and run evals to see if performance holds up.

As models have gotten smarter, improving agent architecture is becoming less about what you can add and more about what you can delete.

https://t.co/DNq60Skkmc

Terms every AI product builder should know.

A few years ago, only ML engineers needed to know these. Now, across 113 PM job postings I look at, 76% want you to know AI.

tweet_headlines.headline: Every Mac on macOS 27 now has a __free offline LLM in Terminal__ via `fm` — no account, API key, or internet connection required.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Every Mac on macOS 27 now has a free LLM built into the Terminal.

No account. No API key. No internet. No token bill.

Setup (1 minute):

1. sudo fm license (enter your Mac password, one time)
2. fm available (checks the model is downloaded)
3. fm respond “your question”

Works on any Apple Silicon Mac, M1 included.

- Pipe files: cat notes.txt | fm respond -i “summarize this”
- Get JSON back: build a schema with fm schema object, pass it with --schema
- Local API: fm serve gives you an OpenAI-compatible endpoint on localhost
- Resume chats: sessions save to ~/.fm/sessions/

The limit is 4,096 tokens per session, and your prompt, instructions, and the answer all share it.

So skip code and math. Use it for summarizing, extracting, classifying, and rewriting.

Free, private, offline, and already on your Mac.

tweet_headlines.author: Mike_Scully_
tweet_headlines.headline: Mike Scully makes the case that __hourly pricing for AI work punishes speed__ — charge 20–30% of the annual value you're replacing instead.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
Stop charging by the hour for AI work.

Here’s why it’s costing you.

Say you build an automation in 4 hours that saves a business 10 hours a week. At $50 an hour, you’d charge $200.

But look at it from the business owner’s side. Those 10 hours a week add up to over 500 hours a year. If the person doing that work costs them $25 an hour, that’s more than $12,500 a year they’re spending on a problem you just fixed.

You charged $200 for something worth $12,500 to them.

That’s the problem with hourly pricing for AI work. The better you get, the faster you build, and the less you earn. You’re punished for being good at it.

So price it by the value instead:

Ask how many hours a week the task takes, and who’s doing it.
Work out what that costs them over a year.
Charge somewhere between 20% and 30% of that.

In this example, that’s $2,500 to $3,750. The client still saves thousands in the first year, and every year after that it’s pure saving for them.

When you put it that way, $3,000 is an easy decision for them. $200 makes you look like you don’t know what it’s worth either.

Price the problem you solve. How long it took you to build is your business, not theirs.
